The Supreme Court keeps insisting that no President is a king, then handing Trump powers that increasingly resemble a royal exemption from accountability. Trump's ballroom is one key example. Even the Chief Justice suggested it is "likely illegal."

In Trump v. United States, the Court’s conservative majority created absolute criminal immunity for a President’s core constitutional acts and presumptive immunity for other official acts. That was an extraordinary expansion of presidential protection.

Now a Postal Service whistleblower alleges officials continued developing Trump’s mail ballot system even after a federal judge ordered the plan halted. If proven, that is not some procedural disagreement. Court orders are commands, not suggestions.

This is where the Supreme Court’s credibility is tested. If executive officials can push ahead until litigation catches up, while the Court repeatedly resolves cases through immunity, jurisdiction, standing or emergency orders, then “rule of law” becomes a slogan.

So here is the question for the justices: What exactly are you prepared to do when an administration ignores a federal court?

Those robes confer authority, not immunity from accountability. A Supreme Court unwilling to defend judicial orders risks turning itself into the punch line of the constitutional system it is supposed to protect.

Here are some of those changes. While they apply worldwide, they are more applicable in richer, more populous, or larger countries.

1. Stop, then reverse the increased maldistribution of income and wealth. Steps: Major tax changes, better auditing, simplification of tax codes.

2. Accelerate the substitution of renewable energy for fossil fuel energy. 

3. Reverse the increasing debt levels, not only of governments (the biggest borrowers) but of individuals (debt for big-ticket items like medical care, higher education, and housing). This goes hand-in-hand with #1 above.

4. Reduce military spending. Decide that some basic necessities require government spending, either in the first place, or more than is now being spent - again medical care, higher education, and housing.

5. Reduce, reuse, and recycle materials to a greater extent than now. Ideally, reduce waste (defined as anything which cannot be further used) as close to zero as possible.

6. Country-by-country political reform, to reduce the influence of the wealthy in superficially democratic systems, and to push authoritarian systems toward democracy.

When there are so many unknowns about what consciousness is and how it works, how can we be so certain that AI systems don’t exhibit some degree of it? If the history of consciousness research teaches us anything, it’s that humans disregard the possibility of consciousness in other beings, see our treatment of animals. What if we’re doing the same now?

I have no idea if today’s AI systems are conscious, but I would never claim that it’s impossible to reach. More and more it’s undeniable these systems are intelligent, or at least approximate intelligence to a high degree. At a certain point when does a sufficiently detailed approximation of intelligence warrant the consideration of consciousness? I don’t know the answer but then nobody else does either, so maybe we should avoid such definitive claims.

Conversation With An American Writer

'You have courage, ' they tell me.

branding the hacks, the would-be writers.

comments.name: Mike Mc Cowan

Priceless.  

Universities demand transparency from corporations, politicians, taxpayers—and probably the cafeteria vending machine. But ask who’s funding THEM and suddenly everyone discovers a constitutional right to privacy.

30 days. Release every foreign source, every university, every dollar, every agreement and every condition attached. Failure to comply? Statutory penalties and loss of federal funds where the law permits.

comments.body:
What this actually suggests is the cash-laden players are acting as affordable lenders, funding those downstream who are running up against expensive capital, bid up by Trump's war and AI itself. As per Benzinga's "The $100 Billion Debt Warning":

"In its latest weekly commentary, BlackRock highlighted growing financial strain downstream in the AI ecosystem. The firm warned that hyperscalers are running down their cash reserves and leaning heavily on debt markets. “U.S. hyperscaler investment-grade bond issuance has topped $100 billion this year, more than twice the 2025 total,” the report noted.

Because of higher interest rates and massive capital requirements, BlackRock advises investors to “look beyond the AI model race for more opportunities as capital gets more expensive.”" 

That's the ecosystem that NVIDIA is lending in. The cash-rich are investing in the cash-poor because they understand the industry, and have faith in the outcome. And what that also does externally is: it takes some of the demand pressure off of outside financing.

The bulk of NVIDIA's receivables are owed by mega-cap hyperscalers which carry near-zero default risk. So that is what allows Nvidia to make these type of investments. Usually eating donuts or something because there were no dine-in restaurants in California. You can't tell the full story of bollards without how delightful they were at that time.

comments.name: Jack Frost
comments.body:
The Commonwealth of PA installed bollards, many of them retractable at driveways such as the entrance to the state capitol or plazas at the capitol where crowds may gather such as at the fountains at the rear of the state capitol.  
The retractable bollards require maintenance and in some cases 24/7 guards to access switches.  
While these barriers seem to provide protection the reality is that in most cases they are useless.  Some are placed so that they can easily be driven around and certainly people on foot or motorcycles can breeze past the barriers.  
The bollards may be prudent but the reality of the little protection they provide makes them more of a sign of paranoia, not real security for buildings or people.  
We are already distant from many of our representatives and the civil servants who are charged with public safety and this physical barrier is just one more wall between the people and government.  
Do we really need to have fortress like structures everywhere?

They would form alliances and it was usually but not always, the dog and the ferret vs. the cat.  The dog and the ferret seemed to have a sense of humor whereas the cat appeared to have none. As a result they would stage ambushes on the cat sometimes quite ingeniously and comically (to human observers).  Endlessly entertaining.

comments.name: Lisa Reinke
comments.body:
I loved my pet ferrets.  Here’s my knowledge to convey:

They are like kittens that never grow up.  Adorable, playful, funny and curious about everything.

They learn their name, recognize and love you, and can be trained to not nip, use a litter box, and come running when a toy is squeaked.

If you keep their bedding and cage clean, they do not stink.  They do smell faintly musky.

I once caught a wild baby mink on accident by chirruping and moving my fingers.  I thought it was a lost ferret.  Weasels are super curious.

You must watch them with toddlers.  Ferrets like dragging kits to safety by the nape.  Something about crying makes ferrets want to move the sound to a safe place - like under the couch.  Ferrets can injure young children.  They also will kill birds.  They are not the pet for children under age 8.

Ferrets burn bright.  When awake, they are full speed adorable.  When tired they fall into a deep slumber wherever they stop.  You must put them to bed or you may accidentally tread on them, causing injuries.

They  get into everything.  They can open cabinets, climb furniture, discover small openings under baseboards.  You have to ferret proof your home.  Our ferrets were all right-handed, except for one lefty.  

They live short lives.  You will love them like a dog or cat, but you get eight years of companionship if you are lucky.  Their passing will break your heart, the same as dogs and cats.  I couldn’t take the sorrow of their short lifespan.

I’m from Aliquippa and I worked in that steel mill, as did my father. It was once one of the largest in the world. As I started reading this, I thought, “Uh oh. Look out Quip town.” And there it was, four or five paragraphs down. 

That tiny city, like so many others in the area, has been eviscerated over the past half century. Most of downtown Aliquippa has been bulldozed. The hospital I was born in was built by the union and was also closed and demolished in just the last decade. 

That union, Local 1211 of the USW, was instrumental in establishing workers rights to organize in this country due to the Labor Relations Board suing J&L Steel on behalf of the striking Aliquippa workers and the SCOTUS ruling in favor of the workers by upholding the Wagner Act in 1937. 

The people of that area, and that town in particular, have an incredible amount of pride. Aliquippa’s football and basketball teams have won more state championships than any other town in Pennsylvania. They know their past history of a thriving economy in the glory days of the steel industry. 

They are desperate. Big industry coming to town has been for decades their only hope. They’re going to latch onto this data center idea like there’s no tomorrow. You won’t be able to convince them that its builders won’t be local, that the facility will run on a skeleton crew of technicians, also not locals, or that the center itself will make their lives not better, but worse. 

These are things they could not imagine.

comments.body:
Like many here, I’ve had a Grand Canyon experience, but mine also included a flood.  In Sept. 1980 we were camped in the NPS campground near Phantom Ranch when a mid morning thunderstorm caught us preparing for a day hike.  Our deluge lasted only 20 minutes, but delivered over an inch of precipitation, much of it as 1 cm hail so intense it looked like fog.  The deafening noise of the hail plus dancing in several inches of flowing ice water made us almost miss the mudslide into our campsite.  Fortunately we escaped serious damage, but our neighbors downstream had gone hiking for the day and lost everything from their site.

As things cleared we witnessed one of the most amazing sights I’ve seen anywhere, including my travels to nearly 3/4 of our NPs.  The storm also hit the upper canyon, and as we surveyed the damage at our level, we looked up to see perhaps a dozen waterfalls cascading over the edge of the Tonto Platform 1500 feet above.  Their first drop was 1-200 vertical feet, then down into the inner canyon to the Colorado River.  A half hour later they were gone and one would never have suspected such a thing had happened.

The rangers imposed martial law and put us all into Phantom Ranch overnight so trail damage/safety could be assessed.  The next morning we made it to the North Rim, 14 miles horizontal and over a mile up, in 2.5 hours, powered mostly by fear.  Never again would I question the role of water in sculpting the desert environment.

comments.name: FISSIONFUSION

Possibly the most awesome place on earth, for me anyway. I never use the word "awesome," but awe struck I was at the age of 20 in 1973.

Rick & I decided to quit our jobs and buy Ameripasses, which provided 30 days of unlimited travel on Greyhound busses in the US, Mexico and Canada for $150. First stop, you guessed it: GC, AZ.

Arrived mid-afternoon, pitched our tent, ate and prepared for a bit of hiking the following day. 

The Grand Canyon is as unforgiving as it is beautiful. Early that morning we ate and hiked into the canyon at the south end; sunny and cool for May and rather eventless going in. But, the hike out is more of a hike up; never ending and up. We rested at least a million times and drank as much as we could. Those riding mules had no idea what they missed. 

Got to the top and B-lined to the tent. Next morning I woke up to find that my blisters had blisters.

If you make this trip, do your homework. And, talk to everyone you know who's done it. We survived and made our way out to Monterrey, up to San Francisco to Tahoe and back, to Eugene to Port Angeles, to Vancouver to Banff, Alberta and back home. Unforgettable. But the high point was the Grand Canyon.

So sorry for those who didn't survive this tragedy.  And, so happy for those who did. 

Due respect to Mother Nature and Father Time.

It was arduous, painful and intimidating, but my 72 year old knees made it. The Red Wall at sunset is breathtaking. Camping by Bright Angel Creek with the sound of the Colorado nearby, magical. But there is always present the knowledge that the Canyon has wicked teeth, and its incredible beauty can quickly turn against even the well prepared. 

I feel for those lost and injured. And we should all recognize the trauma of Rangers and first responders who are called to deal with tragedies as this. No one should go into the Canyon without acknowledging the potential for danger. And to be prepared to take care of yourself and others.

comments.body:
There will be a thousand thousand stories of loss as the ramifications of climate change begin to mount.
And for every story told, there will be countless others of creatures suffering and disappearing beyond the horizon of our awareness. And what does that really mean? It means that I can get a glimpse of this loss, feel it in my gut, at least until something else pulls my attention away. I can feel it like a physical weight, and yet even as someone who spent a decade fighting pipeline expansion in the midwest,  I nonetheless happily drove an hour last week to go go-kart racing with my son. The contradictions within the walls of my mind announce regularly and to nobody that  I am a house divided against myself. And you could write a strong response against me for that, and you'd be right. And if you looked in the mirror and asked yourself about everything you've bought or done or inflicted on this planet, you'd likely find those same contradictions. Individually and in tiny groups, we're sometimes capable of brilliant things, and yet collectively we're a ball of heat gathering speed for a crash we've long seen coming.
Even as the systems to which we are stuck fast refuse to budge from the wheel-ruts leading us to our destruction, we understand that they are systems of our own making; that they could be, and still can be altered.
And yet on we go anyway, wrecking this eden for all the creatures of the earth, a tragedy only amplified by our awareness that this is the case.

The wonder that is these reefs and the magnificent life they house is so much more awe-inspring than AI or any technology could ever be. Can we stop warming before it hits 2C?

Yeah OK I 'get' that it's hard to state categorically that one hurricane/flood/heatwave is due to a 0.5C (for example) rise in temperature, but many, many such events all over the world? In 1970, an earthquake of 7.9 intensity rattled the province of Ancash, Perú, for 45 seconds, causing widespread destruction in the region. High above Yungay, a city in the Callejón de Huaylas, the quake shook loose a large piece of glacier and a piece of rock from Nevado Huascáran, the highest mountain in Perú. The resulting mudflow buried Yungay, some 13 kilometres away from the point of origin in about two minutes, and killed approximately 25,000 people. Many media in the U.S. exercise caution and prudence in reporting victims of crimes and of natural disasters with respect to providing identities, addresses, and families of  victims, unless the persons so affected agree to the publication.  Often however, many media report discussions with victims without providing to viewers assurances that the victims agree with the publication. 

Even perpetrators of terrible crimes, including teenagers and older ones, often don't have their identities revealed by the media.  For teenage criminals, the lack of names is because of laws governing juveniles.  For adults identified by persons at the scene, the press' failure to report the identities is often concern about libel laws or having the wrong person accused or arrested.

More recently, it has become clear that victim's homes can be be vandalized if it is publicized that they are in a hospital or away from home.  Also, it is often dangerous for victims to have other people know their name and address when they are severely injured at home.

The above can be serious concerns in poverty stricken areas or villages, especially, if police protection is rare.  Finally, there are victims who want to be the ones to make money from their misfortunes, and not the world of people outside who learn of publicity about them. Who can blame them.  Governments differ in how much protection victims get from publicity.  These concerns exist in cases of natural disasters.

We all knew about galliano. History shouldn’t be erased. A proper, well thought out exhibit would have been educational and interesting.

I think the whole thing says more about Anna Wintour and the control that she wields over the event.

Given the state of the country and the economy, the Met Gala she has presided over has become an insult to many. 

The true purpose of a museum extends far beyond simply housing old objects or putting artifacts behind glass. At its core, a museum serves as a dynamic institution dedicated to preserving cultural heritage, fostering public education, and inspiring empathy and critical thinking through shared human experiences.

The Met Gala has become an increasingly tone-deaf, hyper-commercialized spectacle. It’s time to move on to something else.

I respectfully disagree. I go to museum exhibits on a regular basis and consider museums vital for education. Reflection is important, but any observer will note that most people walk around exhibits, taking lots of photos and selfies, but not necessarily reading or engaging in serious reflection on what they have read. Reflection is crucial for an educated society but it's not clear that a costume institute is the place for this type of debate.

It is disingenuous to bring Thomas Jefferson into this discussion. Jefferson, of course, lived more than two centuries ago in a substantively different historical context. Jefferson also helped to launch a new nation as well as set into writing the modern conception of human rights. It's the stark paradoxes of Jefferson's life that make him so thought-provoking as a figure of societal and historical reflection. Galliano, by contrast, is a contemporary designer, who has expressed hateful words for no apparent reason.

comments.name: David B

I, for one, do not look to museums to present hard truths in provocative fashion, precisely because they never have. That's never been their primary role. They are celebrations of some privileged perspective or another and they cannot help but be so because of the expense involved in founding and maintaining them. Elites, whatever their background or stated goals, promote themselves. Period. This essay is evidence of this. It says nothing more than, "we dabblers in the criticism of elite culture are still relevant!" No one really cares about high fashion, the Met Gala, or the struggles of the elite to distinguish themselves from one another through gross acts of conspicuous consumption except maybe Robin Givhan. No one looks to the world of high fashion or elitist museums to reveal the dark hearts that beat within us all.

Because both major parties are "pro-business" parties (although that's much more true for Republicans than Democrats), the law has generally protected businesses from being held accountable for externalities -- those downstream effects that come from the use of their products. 

There has been some attempt to limit the effects of production, in pollution controls, for example, but the externalities produced by the use of the products has been seen as the responsibility of the users (consumers). But when businesses use their power to limit the options (e.g., opposing robust public transportation) and lure consumers into believing their products are safe when the companies are well aware of the impacts, then it only seems sensible to hold the companies accountable for the impacts of the use of their products.

comments.name: Kurts
comments.body:
As noted in this article: "The so-called polluter pays principle is also central to the [federal] 'superfund' laws" on which the NY law is largely based.

The "polluter pays principle" is well founded given that polluters should have to pay for what economists call "externalities" -- for example, the harmful emissions from an industrial facility. Indeed, carbon taxes and cap-and-trade emissions markets aim to do just that in a relatively concise manner. It's far trickier to calculate and pursue broader "damages" like New York's law seeks to do.

In this case, the judge appears to have ruled that New York's "sweeping statute" violated the supremacy clause by surpassing "limits of state law." Instead of swinging for the the fences, states and other plaintiffs would be well advised to play small ball to avoid the supremacy clause's reach.

comments.name: C

This article has a dangerously inaccurate description of the What3Words app. All that W3W does is convert your longitude and latitude into a 3-word phrase using a proprietary algorithm. Your phone already measures your longitude and latitude without W3W, so the app adds no new functionality. Nor can it measure your position any more accurately than your phone.

In a backcountry emergency, rescuers will want your longitude and latitude, not a proprietary 3-word code for your position from an app that they might never have heard of. 

Moreover, the article states that W3W "uses satellites," but the app doesn't add satellite messaging to phones that didn't already have this technical capability. It is critical to understand that GPS satellites (which are used to determine your position) are not communications satellites. Your phone listens to broadcasts from GPS satellites to figure out its position, but it doesn't actually talk to those GPS satellites.

Here in southern Utah, flash floods are very common. What most first-time visitors don't fully appreciate is that flash floods can be triggered by rain that fell hours earlier many miles upstream. You might therefore experience a flash flood even though it didn't rain where you are. This is why it is essential to check the forecast for the upstream watershed of whatever canyon you're hiking in, especially in the monsoon season. 

In Utah, the National Weather Service generates an easy-to understand flash-flood forecast for the major parks (see https://www.weather.gov/slc/flashflood), and it is an excellent resource.

I have two gripes about this article. First, its glowing description of the What3Words app is dangerously wrong (for reasons that I explain in a separate comment that the NYT hasn't posted yet). Second, in many of the areas that are prone to flash floods, it is unrealistic to expect real-time weather updates on your phone because there is very limited (if any) cell service. Flash floods are most dangerous in deep, narrow canyons, and even devices with satellite-messaging capability struggle in that type of terrain. It is far better to scrutinize the forecast ahead of time and to err on the side of caution if the forecast looks iffy.

comments.name: Liemba
comments.body:
Thank you for the fascinating article. Much respect and admiration go out to the medical professionals and humanitarian workers. I hope the situation improves soon.

This might be slightly off-topic, but perhaps still relevant to readers in the U.S. If I am not mistaken, funeral expenses including casket costs can only be deducted on the estate tax returns of the deceased, which are usually filed only by the wealthy. Personally, I feel that funeral expenses, including the costs of burial and coffins, should be allowed to be deducted by the living family members who pay for them, which would serve to extend more equitable treatment to taxpayers who are not as financially fortunate. Even if this change to the tax code were to occur, I suspect most people would still end up choosing cremation due to cost burdens. However, I think this type of policy change would be a step in the right direction, providing a little bit of financial relief for surviving families. If necessary, these proposed changes could be funded by eliminating many non-essential deduction items that primarily favor a smaller portion of the population - the upper-middle class and above in particular.

The South Rim receives its water via a trans-canyon pipeline from Roaring Springs, which is near the North Rim. The routing of the pipeline takes it through Bright Angel Canyon, where the most severe flooding was. comments.name: Realist
comments.body: The buildings at my alma mater, a large university in the temperate climate zone, were at one time all heated by a central steam system. Tunnels extended from the steam plant to each of the buildings. The steam was turned on in mid autumn, and turned off again in mid spring. When the tunnels were not full of steam, it was considered a fair sport to get into the system and venture around campus. Sometimes this was done in search of a woman’s dormitory, but most of the time it was just something to do. I wonder whether something similar is going on here.
